name: Upturned nose preference

card.summary: The debate over whether a rotated-up nasal tip is the most attractive nose shape, which guides rhinoplasty tip-rotation goals and how some people read their own profile.
card.note: Over-rotation is described by surgeons as harder to correct than under-rotation.

quick.overview:
An upturned nose is one whose tip is rotated upward, which opens the angle between nose and upper lip and shows more of the nostrils from the front. Many people see a slight upturn as more attractive, and rhinoplasty surgeons often aim for some tip rotation, particularly in women.

On looksmax forums the topic is argued in terms of nostril show, masculinity and jaw structure. Published research is mainly preference studies of edited profile images that report a range of preferred nasolabial angles, differing by sex and population.
quick.how: In practice people compare their profile photos with target angles, and those considering surgery discuss tip rotation with a rhinoplasty surgeon. Forum users also link upward nasal rotation to upper-jaw (maxilla) position and discuss jaw surgery that rotates the maxilla counterclockwise.
quick.risks: Surgical tip rotation carries the general risks of rhinoplasty. Surgeons describe over-rotation, which shows excessive nostril and gives an operated look, as harder to fix than under-rotation. Preferences vary with sex, age and culture, so there is no single accepted ideal.

lead: An upturned nose, or rotated tip, describes a nasal tip that angles upward in profile. The measurement most often used is the nasolabial angle between the columella and the upper lip, which the plastic surgery literature gives as roughly 90 to 95 degrees in men and 100 to 105 degrees in women [1].

For appearance, a modest upturn is often treated as a youthful, feminine and open-looking feature, and tip rotation is a standard goal in rhinoplasty. In looksmaxxing communities it is debated as an ideal in itself, with some users arguing for exposed nostrils tied to maxillary growth and others calling a pronounced upturn undesirable [2][3][4].
Research consists mainly of preference studies using altered profile silhouettes or photographs, which report preferred angles that vary by sex, location and study [5].

chain: Tip rotated upward or nasolabial angle opened
Profile reads as more open and youthful
Nose appears more balanced with the face
angle.text: Tip rotation, achieved surgically or discussed as a target in profile analysis, changes the nasolabial angle and how much of the nostrils shows from the front. Practitioners and forum users use angle ranges as reference points for what looks balanced.

paras: Profile analysis separates tip rotation from other nasal features. Textbook-style guidance describes the dorsum as straight, columella show of about 2 mm, a nasofrontal angle of about 115 to 130 degrees and a nasolabial angle that is more open in women than men [1]. A 'ski slope' nose is a related shape with a concave dorsum that continues down to an upturned tip, a distinction forum users make themselves [4].

Rhinoplasty can rotate the tip by reshaping cartilage or adjusting the columella, and surgical guidelines describe tip projection and rotation as part of balancing the nose with the chin and lips [1]. A surgeon's commentary cited in the literature holds that an over-rotated tip is a harder problem to correct secondarily than an under-rotated one, though this is professional opinion rather than a controlled finding.

Studies of edited faces report varying ideals. One general-population study found most aesthetic nasolabial angles of about 105 degrees for female and 97 degrees for male profiles, while a 2023 Turkish study reported means of about 91 degrees for women and 95 degrees for men; the literature's normal range of 90 to 115 degrees is described as somewhat arbitrary .

A multinational study of laypeople in seven locations altered lip and nose position in millimetre steps and found that profile preferences were influenced by factors that include where raters lived [5]. Many studies rely on digitally altered images and convenience samples.

A looksmax.org thread argues that an upturned nose with exposed nostrils reflects healthy maxillary growth and counterclockwise maxillary rotation, linking it to better airflow and citing before-and-after examples of jaw surgery [2]. Replies dispute this, distinguishing nasolabial angle from a visibly upturned nose and calling the latter undesirable [2]. Other threads argue that a slight tip upturn without front-facing nostril show looks good on men, and debate whether an upturned nose reads as feminine given how many models have one [3][4].

Studies are mainly perception studies rather than clinical trials. A 2023 multinational study had laypeople rate altered profile silhouettes [5], and the preference literature on the nasolabial angle reports sex-specific ideals . A 2019 web survey of 503 participants rated edited male photographs with different angle combinations on attractiveness, health and masculinity . Separately, clinical genetics literature notes that a short, upturned nose is a feature of several syndromes, such as fetal alcohol syndrome [6].

lore.intro: The upturned nose is argued over on looksmax.org as both an ideal and a flaw, usually tied to maxilla position.

claims.claim: An upturned nose and exposed nostrils are ideal because they signal healthy maxilla growth
claims.believers: A forum author says counterclockwise maxillary rotation and wider maxilla create an upturn and better breathing, citing surgery examples [2].
claims.experts: Preference studies report ideal nasolabial angles but do not test the maxilla link; surgeons describe over-rotation as hard to fix .

claims.claim: A slight tip upturn looks good, but a visible upturn with front nostril show looks bad on men
claims.believers: Forum users say a subtle tip rotation without exposed nostrils reads best on men [3].
claims.experts: One study found men are less tolerant of an open nasolabial angle than women .
